title: Passwords, Passkeys & MFA
summary: Build logins that are easy for you and hard for attackers.

lessons.title: Length beats complexity
points: Current NIST guidance (SP 800-63B-4, 2025) asks for at least 15 characters when a password is the only sign-in factor.
It also says systems must not force character-mix rules or routine password changes. Change a password when there's evidence it was compromised.
A passphrase of several random words, like "Tulip-Ladder-Ocean-Pocket", is long, memorable and strong.

lessons.title: One account, one password
points: Reusing a password means one breached website can unlock your email, bank and work accounts. Attackers test leaked passwords everywhere ("credential stuffing").
A password manager creates and remembers a unique password for every site. You only remember one strong master passphrase.
Password managers also help against phishing: they won't autofill on a look-alike domain.

lessons.title: Turn on MFA
points: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) adds a second proof: something you have (phone, security key) or something you are (fingerprint).
Any MFA is much better than none. SMS codes are one of the weakest forms because of SIM-swap and interception.
Never share an MFA code. Nobody legitimate, including IT support, needs to ask for it.

lessons.title: Passkeys & phishing-resistant MFA
points: Passkeys and hardware security keys use FIDO2/WebAuthn. The login is tied to the real website, so a fake site can't capture or reuse it.
CISA calls phishing-resistant MFA the gold standard, and says FIDO/WebAuthn is the only widely available form of it.
Watch for "MFA fatigue": repeated approval prompts you didn't trigger. Deny them and report it, because someone has your password.
lessons.tip: If a site offers passkeys, turn them on. They're stronger and quicker than typing a password.

questions.why: Length matters most. Four random words give a long, hard-to-guess passphrase. The others are short or follow patterns attackers try first.

questions.q: Current NIST guidance recommends forcing everyone to change their password every 90 days.
questions.why: NIST SP 800-63B-4 says verifiers shall not require periodic changes. Passwords should be changed when there's evidence of compromise.

questions.q: Why is reusing the same password on many sites dangerous?
options: A breach on one site lets attackers log in to your other accounts
It makes the password expire faster
questions.why: Attackers take leaked email/password pairs and try them on other services. This is called credential stuffing.

questions.q: Which type of MFA is the most resistant to phishing?
questions.why: FIDO2/WebAuthn credentials are bound to the genuine website's domain, so a fake site can't use them. CISA calls phishing-resistant MFA like this the gold standard.

questions.q: You get 6 MFA approval requests on your phone that you didn't start. What should you do?
options: Approve one to make them stop
Deny them, change your password and report it
questions.why: Unexpected prompts mean someone likely has your password and is trying to wear you down (MFA fatigue). Deny, reset your password and report.

questions.q: A caller from 'IT support' may legitimately ask you to read out your MFA code to fix your account.
questions.why: Never share MFA codes. A real support team doesn't need them, and anyone asking is almost certainly trying to take over your account.

questions.q: What is the main benefit of a password manager?
options: It lets you use one password everywhere
It creates and stores a unique strong password for every account
It removes the need for MFA
questions.why: You get unique, strong passwords everywhere without memorising them, and it won't autofill on look-alike phishing sites.

questions.q: SMS codes are better than having no MFA at all.
questions.why: SMS is one of the weakest MFA options because of SIM swapping and interception, but it still blocks many attacks that only use stolen passwords.

questions.q: Under NIST SP 800-63B-4, what is the minimum length for a password used as the only sign-in factor?
questions.why: The 2025 revision requires at least 15 characters for single-factor passwords (8 is allowed only when the password is part of multi-factor sign-in).

questions.q: When should you change a password straight away?
options: When you suspect or learn it was exposed or used by someone else
Only when the system forces you
questions.why: Change it when there's evidence or suspicion of compromise, such as a breach notice, a phishing click, or a login you don't recognise.

questions.q: Writing your password on a sticky note on your monitor is fine if your office is locked.
questions.why: Visitors, cleaners, video calls and photos can all expose it. Use a password manager instead.

sources.title: NIST SP 800-63B-4 – Authentication and Authenticator Management (2025)
